title: Binary search trees
summary: Smaller goes left, bigger goes right: inserting and finding by walking down one path, with recursion.

say.never: Picture a guessing game: "I'm thinking of a number. Is it more or less than 50?" Each answer throws away half the numbers. A **binary search tree** stores numbers so you can play that game. Each node holds one number. Everything smaller goes somewhere down its **left** side, and everything bigger goes down its **right** side. To find a number you start at the top and go left or right at each node. You never have to look at the other side.
say.bit: A **binary search tree**: each node has a left side (all smaller) and a right side (all bigger). Finding means walking one path down.

steps.title: A node that links to nodes

say.never: In Java, each node is an object with a number and two **links**: fields that hold other nodes of the same class. A link that holds `null` means "nothing down this way". The tree itself only needs to remember the top node, called the **root**.
say.bit: A node class has fields of its own type for its children; `null` means no child. The tree keeps a link to the root.

say.never: Here's the neat part. The left side of a node is a whole tree on its own, just smaller. So a method that searches a tree can look at one node, then **call itself** on the left or right side. The **base case**, where it stops, is reaching `null`: you walked off the bottom, so the number isn't there.
say.bit: Each side is a smaller tree, so recurse into it. Base case: a `null` link.

board.code:
has(spot, number):
    spot is null?           -> no, it isn't here   (base case)
    number == spot's number -> yes, found it
    number is smaller       -> ask has(smaller side, number)
    otherwise               -> ask has(bigger side, number)

marks.label: the same question, one level down

say.never: Adding a number works the same way: walk down until you hit `null`. That empty spot is where the new node goes. The trick is to make the method **return** the node for the spot it was given. At `null` it returns a brand-new node. Everywhere else it returns the node it already had. The node above saves what comes back into its left or right link, and that's how the new node gets hooked on.
say.bit: Recursive insert returns the node for its spot: a new node at `null`, otherwise the same node, with the caller storing the result in its link.

steps.title: In your lesson: Inserting: hand back the node

say.never: In `TeamTree`, the node class is `TeamNode`, with `team_`, `left_` and `right_`. Write a **helper** for each job: a `private` method that takes a `TeamNode` and calls itself. The public method just starts it at `root_`. For insert, store what the helper returns back into `root_`, so the first team becomes the root. A team that's already there goes neither left nor right, so it isn't added twice.
say.bit: Write private helpers that take a `TeamNode`; the public methods start them at `root_`. Equal teams aren't added again.
